chapters.name: Chapter 1: Principles and preparing land without ploughing

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The three principles of conservation agriculture
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify whether a field follows each of the three principles of conservation agriculture.
This lesson builds toward: Looking at a field or a description of one, you will identify whether it follows each of the three principles of conservation agriculture, naming all three as FAO describes them, including at least 30 percent soil cover.
Conservation agriculture (CA) is a way of farming that protects the soil so it holds more of the little rain that falls. FAO describes three principles that work together.
1. Minimum soil disturbance: no ploughing. Seed and fertilizer go into the soil through small holes, basins or narrow rip lines, and the rest of the soil is left alone. 2. Permanent soil cover: keep crop residues or cover crops on the surface, covering at least 30 percent of the soil, all year. 3. Crop diversification: rotate or intercrop at least three different crops over time, for example maize, cowpea and sorghum, not maize every year.
Doing one alone helps a little; doing all three together gives the real benefits. Ploughing without cover dries the soil; cover without rotation lets pests build up; no-till with bare soil lets the crust form and rain run off. In dry areas the big gain is water: covered, undisturbed soil lets rain soak in and loses less to the sun.
Words to know:
- Conservation agriculture (CA): farming with minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and crop diversification.
- Tillage: turning or breaking the soil, for example by ploughing or digging.
- Crop residues: the stalks, leaves and husks left after harvest.
- Crust: a hard skin that forms on bare soil after rain and stops water soaking in.
Official sources:
- FAO: Conservation Agriculture (definition and the three principles)
Try it now: Walk one of your fields. For each principle, write yes, partly or no: Is it ploughed? How much of the soil is covered (estimate in percent)? How many different crops grew there in the last three seasons? Circle the principle that is weakest.
You can now name the three principles of conservation agriculture and check a field against each.

check.q: Which is one of FAO's three principles of conservation agriculture?
options: Burning residues to clean the field
Permanent soil cover of at least 30 percent
Growing the same crop every year
check.why: FAO lists minimum disturbance, permanent soil cover (at least 30 percent) and crop diversification.

check.q: A farmer stopped ploughing but leaves the soil bare and grows maize every year. What is missing?
check.why: Without cover and rotation, no-till alone gives few of the benefits.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Planting basins and zai pits
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Mark out and dig planting basins or zai pits with manure in each, before the rains.
This lesson builds toward: On one field before the rains, you will mark out and dig planting basins or zai pits with manure or compost in each, in rows across the slope, dug in the dry season.
Planting basins and zai pits are small holes dug by hand where the crop is planted. Only the basin is disturbed; the soil between is left covered. Each basin catches rain and holds the manure or compost right where the roots are.
Zai pits come from farmers in Burkina Faso and Niger, who used them to bring hard, crusted land back into millet and sorghum. WOCAT describes pits of roughly 30 to 40 cm across and 10 to 15 cm deep, in staggered rows across the slope, about 10,000 a hectare, with manure or compost in each. Planting basins used in southern and eastern Africa are similar: small, regular holes in rows, dug to the same spacing each year so you return to the same spots.
Dig them in the dry season after harvest, when there is less other work, so you can plant with the first good rains instead of waiting to plough. Put the soil from the pit on the downhill side to catch more water. Add a handful or two of manure or compost in each basin and cover it lightly. Ask your extension officer for the spacing used for your crop in your area.
It is hard work, especially the first year. Dig a part of the field each week, share labour in a group, and reuse the same basins in later seasons, which is much quicker.
Step by step:
- Choose the field and mark rows across the slope with string or sticks.
- Mark basin spots at the spacing extension recommends for your crop.
- Dig in the dry season; pile soil on the downhill side.
- Add manure or compost in each basin and cover lightly.
- Leave the soil between basins covered.
- Plant in the basins with the first good rains.
Words to know:
- Planting basin: a small hole dug by hand where seed and manure go, leaving the rest of the soil undisturbed.
- Zai pit: a planting pit filled with manure or compost, first used by farmers in Burkina Faso and Niger to restore crusted land.
- Across the slope: along the contour, so rows catch water instead of channelling it downhill.
Official sources:
- WOCAT: Zai or tassa planting pits (Niger)
- FAO: Conservation Agriculture (definition and the three principles)
Try it now: On a small part of a field (for example 10 m by 10 m), mark rows across the slope and dig five basins or zai pits. Time how long each takes, add manure, and work out how many days the whole field would take.
You can now mark out and dig planting basins or zai pits with manure, across the slope, before the rains.

check.q: When should you dig planting basins or zai pits?
options: Only when it is raining hard
At harvest time, on top of the crop
In the dry season before the rains
check.why: Digging early lets you plant with the first good rains and spreads the work.

check.q: Where should the soil from a zai pit go?
options: On the downhill side of the pit, to catch more water
Back into the pit straight away
check.why: A small ridge downhill helps each pit catch and hold runoff.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Ripping and direct seeding
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose between basins, ripping and direct seeding for one of your fields.
This lesson builds toward: Given your soil, labour, draught power and rainfall, you will choose between basins, ripping and direct seeding for a field, giving at least two reasons for the choice.
Basins suit hand-hoe farmers on small plots. If you have oxen or can hire a tractor, a ripper or a direct seeder can cover more land with less labour.
A ripper is a narrow tine, often fitted to an ox-plough beam in place of the mouldboard, that opens a narrow slot (a rip line) for seed and fertilizer, leaving the soil between rows covered. Ripping in the dry season can also break a hard layer under the surface (a plough pan) so roots and water go deeper. Direct seeding puts seed straight through the residues with a jab planter (a hand tool) or an animal- or tractor-drawn seeder, with no opening of lines at all.
Which to choose? Think about your labour (basins need the most), draught power (ripping needs oxen or a tractor), soil (hard, crusted soils benefit from basins or ripping), and field size. Trials across Zambia from 2006 to 2015 compared basins, ripping and direct seeding with mouldboard ploughing on real farms. Ask your extension officer or a CA project where you can see these tools working, and whether they can be hired.
Step by step:
- Write your field size, labour and access to oxen or a tractor.
- Check the soil: is there a hard layer or crust?
- Small plot and hand labour: basins.
- Oxen or tractor and hard soil: ripping.
- Good residues and a seeder available: direct seeding.
- Ask extension where to see and hire the tools.
Words to know:
- Ripper: a narrow tine pulled by oxen or a tractor that opens a slot for seed without turning the soil.
- Plough pan: a hard layer just below the ploughed depth that blocks roots and water.
- Jab planter: a hand tool pushed into the ground to place seed (and sometimes fertilizer) through residues.
- Direct seeding: planting straight into undisturbed soil and residues.
Official sources:
- CIMMYT: Conservation agriculture on-farm trials in Zambia (basins, ripping, direct seeding vs ploughing, 2006-2015)
- FAO: Conservation Agriculture (definition and the three principles)
Try it now: For your chosen field, write the field size, your labour, your access to oxen or a tractor, and how hard the soil is. Choose basins, ripping or direct seeding and write two reasons for your choice.
You can now choose between basins, ripping and direct seeding for a field, with reasons.

check.q: A farmer has 3 hectares, a pair of oxen and hard soil. Which method fits best?
options: Hand-dug basins on all 3 hectares in one week
check.why: Oxen and hard soil suit ripping, which covers more land than hand basins.

options: A hand tool that places seed through residues
check.why: A jab planter lets you plant directly into covered, undisturbed soil.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: The season and the transition

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Managing mulch and residues
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan how to keep at least 30 percent of a field covered all year.
This lesson builds toward: For a field under conservation agriculture, you will plan how to keep the soil covered and control weeds without ploughing, keeping at least 30 percent cover and using only registered herbicides as the label says, if any.
Cover is the principle farmers find hardest, because residues have other uses: animals graze fields after harvest, and stalks are used for fuel, fencing and building. In dry areas, termites can also eat surface residues.
Plan for it. Decide how much residue stays on the field and how much goes to animals. Cut and store some stover for dry-season feed so animals are not let onto the CA field. Talk with neighbours and herders about the field: some communities agree that marked CA fields are not grazed, or the farmer fences a small field with live fences or thorn branches. Grow cover from other sources: an intercrop of cowpea or lablab, grass from field edges, or prunings from trees.
To check cover, look straight down at a square metre in several places and estimate how much soil you cannot see. You want at least 30 percent covered (FAO); more is better. Spread residues evenly, not in heaps, and leave them on top rather than burying them.
Never burn residues on a CA field. Burning removes the cover and organic matter you are building.
Step by step:
- Decide the share of residues for cover and for feed.
- Cut and store feed so animals stay off the CA field.
- Agree with neighbours and herders, or fence the field.
- Add cover from intercrops, edge grass or tree prunings.
- Check cover: look down at a square metre in several places.
- Spread evenly; never burn.
Words to know:
- Mulch: material spread on the soil surface to cover and protect it.
- Stover: the dried stalks and leaves of maize or sorghum after harvest.
- Live fence: a row of shrubs or trees planted close together to keep animals out.
Official sources:
- FAO: Conservation Agriculture (definition and the three principles)
- FAO: The importance of soil organic matter
Try it now: Estimate the cover on your chosen field today in three spots. Write where extra cover will come from, how much stover goes to animals, and how you will keep animals off the field (agreement, fence or stored feed).
You can now plan how to keep at least 30 percent of a CA field covered, while still feeding your animals.

check.q: Neighbours' cattle graze all the residues off your CA field every dry season. What can help?
options: Agree with herders, fence the field, or store feed so animals stay off
check.why: Community agreements, fences and stored feed protect the cover.

check.q: How do you check whether a field has enough cover?
options: Look down at a square metre in several places and estimate the share of soil hidden
check.why: A quick visual estimate in several spots shows whether cover reaches 30 percent.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Controlling weeds without ploughing
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan weed control for a CA field without ploughing.
This lesson builds toward: For a field under conservation agriculture, you will plan how to keep the soil covered and control weeds without ploughing, keeping at least 30 percent cover and using only registered herbicides as the label says, if any.
Ploughing buries weeds; without it, weeds can be heavy in the first seasons. This is the main reason farmers give up on CA, so plan weeding from the start.
Weed early and often: the first weeks after the crop comes up matter most. Use a hoe lightly, scraping just below the surface rather than turning the soil, or pull by hand. Never let weeds set seed; every weed that seeds adds thousands for next year. Mulch and a cover crop shade the soil and keep many weeds down, and a dense intercrop leaves less room. Over several seasons of weeding before seeding, the weed seeds in the soil run down and weeding gets easier.
Some CA farmers also use a herbicide. If you do, use only products registered in your country (in Kenya, check the Pest Control Products Board list; in Nigeria, NAFDAC; in Ghana, the Environmental Protection Agency), buy from licensed dealers, and follow the label exactly for the crop, timing and amount. Wear protective clothing, gloves and boots, keep children and animals away, and never spray near water. Ask your extension officer before you start.
Step by step:
- Weed early: the first weeks after emergence.
- Hoe lightly or hand-pull; don't turn the soil.
- Never let weeds set seed.
- Use mulch, cover crops and dense intercrops to shade weeds.
- If using a herbicide: registered product, label, protective equipment.
- Plan labour for weeding before the season starts.
Words to know:
- Weed seed bank: the weed seeds stored in the soil, waiting to grow.
- Herbicide: a chemical that kills weeds.
- Registered product: a pesticide or herbicide approved for use by the national authority.
Official sources:
- Pest Control Products Board, Kenya (registered products)
- NAFDAC, Nigeria (registered agrochemicals)
- Environmental Protection Agency, Ghana (pesticide registration)
- FAO: Conservation Agriculture (definition and the three principles)
Try it now: Write a weed plan for your field: when you will weed (weeks after planting), with what tool, who will do it and how many days it will take, and how cover or an intercrop will help. If you consider a herbicide, write where you will check that it is registered.
You can now plan weed control for a CA field without ploughing, using herbicides only safely and legally if at all.

check.q: Why should you never let weeds set seed in a CA field?
options: Seeds make the crop taste bad
Each seeding weed adds thousands of seeds for next year
check.why: Stopping weeds from seeding runs down the weed seed bank over seasons.

check.q: A farmer in Kenya wants to use a herbicide on her CA maize. What should she check first?
options: That it is registered by the Pest Control Products Board and how the label says to use it
That it is the cheapest bottle
check.why: Only registered products used as the label says, with protective equipment, are safe and legal.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tools, timing, drought years and the transition
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a season calendar of CA jobs, tools and costs, and set up a comparison plot.
This lesson builds toward: For one season on one field, you will write a calendar of every conservation agriculture job with its month, tool and cost, from dry-season preparation to harvest and residue care. Through the first seasons of conservation agriculture, you will compare a conservation agriculture plot with a ploughed plot, recording yield, labour days and costs for both each season.
A CA season starts in the dry season, not at the rains. A typical calendar: after harvest, keep residues and agree on grazing; in the dry season, dig or reuse basins, or rip, and place manure; at the first good rains, plant straight away (no waiting to plough); in the first weeks, weed early and often; during the season, add the intercrop or cover crop; at harvest, leave residues on the field and plan next season's rotation. Next to each job, write the tool (hoe, ripper, jab planter, sprayer and protective gear) and the cost, whether you own, hire or borrow it.
In drought years, CA's main advantage shows. Basins and mulch catch and keep more water, and planting on time uses the early rain. A review of many trials in semi-arid Zimbabwe found that planting basins gave more maize than ploughing in more than half of the trials. But CA does not beat ploughing every year, and it cannot make up for no rain at all.
Expect a transition. Yields may stay the same or even drop in the first one or two seasons while weeds are heavy and the soil adjusts; benefits usually build over several seasons as cover and organic matter grow. Start on one field, keep a ploughed plot beside it, and record yield, labour days and costs for both every season. Judge CA after three seasons, not one.
Step by step:
- List every job from harvest to harvest.
- Put each in a month.
- Add the tool and whether you own, hire or borrow it.
- Add the cost and labour days.
- Mark a ploughed comparison plot of the same size.
- Record yield, labour and cost for both each season; judge after three seasons.
Words to know:
- Transition period: the first seasons after switching to CA, when weeds are heavy and benefits are still building.
- Comparison plot: a plot farmed the old way beside the CA plot, so results can be compared fairly.
- Labour day: one person working for one day; used to measure how much work a job takes.
Official sources:
- Effect of conservation agriculture on maize yield in the semi-arid areas of Zimbabwe (Experimental Agriculture)
- CIMMYT: Conservation agriculture on-farm trials in Zambia (basins, ripping, direct seeding vs ploughing, 2006-2015)
- FAO: Conservation Agriculture (definition and the three principles)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-season CA plan for one field, with a sketch, the land preparation method and reasons, cover and weed plans, the crop and rotation, a month-by-month calendar of jobs, tools and costs, and where your ploughed comparison plot will be.
You can now plan a full CA season with tools, timing and costs, and compare it fairly with ploughing through the transition years.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Three principles The plan still ploughs, leaves soil bare, or grows one crop only. The plan shows minimum disturbance, cover and a rotation or intercrop with at least three crops over time. Explains how the three principles support each other on this field. Land preparation No method chosen, or no reasons. Basins, zai pits, ripping or direct seeding chosen with at least two reasons (labour, power, soil, size). Says where the tools come from and has seen or tried the method. Basins or pits laid out Basins are not across the slope or have no manure plan. Rows across the slope, dry-season digging dates and manure or compost in each basin (if basins or pits are used). Has dug a test area, timed it and worked out labour for the whole field. Cover and weeds No plan for residues, grazing or weeds. Keeps at least 30 percent cover, deals with grazing, and has a weeding schedule; any herbicide is registered and used as labelled with protective equipment. Adds a cover crop or intercrop and a plan to stop weeds seeding. Season calendar Jobs are missing or have no dates. Every job from dry-season preparation to harvest, with month, tool and cost. Includes labour days and who does each job. Comparison through the transition No comparison plot or records. A ploughed comparison plot, with yield, labour days and costs to record each season. Commits to judging after three seasons and lists what would make them change the plan. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the plan and try again.

check.q: When does the work for a CA season begin?
options: In the dry season, after the last harvest
At the first rain, with ploughing
At harvest of the next crop
check.why: Basins, ripping, manure and residue plans are done in the dry season so you can plant with the first rains.

check.q: Your CA plot gives the same yield as the ploughed plot in season one. What should you do?
options: Keep recording for at least three seasons before judging
check.why: Benefits build over several seasons; one season is too early to judge.
